notes.decision: Translated as imperative 'take charge over yourselves' — Greek ἄρχω ('rule, take charge') with 2pl reflexive ⲧⲏⲛⲉ. The construction with ⲙ̄ⲡⲕⲱⲧⲉ as adverbial complement gives 'exercise rule in/over the encompassing of the bodily men' — the apostolic-pastoral charge over the bodily community of disciples.

ⲛⲉ taken as negative future-prohibitive: 'so that Sin shall not become strong.' The whole Sin-clause governs five consecutive ⲛϥ̄- conjunctives describing what Sin would do if it prevailed: take light, scatter forth, spread forth.
Rendered 'from the All to the All' — the doubled ⲡⲧⲏⲣϥ̄ functions as merism for total/complete preparation, paralleling Manichaean cosmic-totality vocabulary already in glossary.
ⲧⲟ̄ⲓⲛⲭⲧⲟ analyzed as Lyc. action-noun ⲧⲟ̄ⲓⲛ- (cf. ⲧⲟⲓⲛⲃⲱⲗ, ⲧⲟ̄ⲓⲛ†ⲟⲩⲱ in glossary) on ⲭⲧⲟ = ϫⲡⲟ 'beget.' The chapter title is thus 'the begetting of Adam.' Distinguished from homophonous ⲕⲧⲟ 'turn.'

Three distinct verbs of fashioning preserved: ⲡⲗⲁⲥⲥⲉ 'mold' (πλάσσω, archonic fashioning), ϩⲱⲅⲣⲁⲫⲉ 'depict/paint' (ζωγραφέω, image-painting), ⲭⲡⲟ 'beget' (ϫⲡⲟ, generative birth). The catechumen's question parses Adam's origin into these three registers.

Parsed as relative perfect ⲛ̄ⲧⲁ-ⲛ-(ⲧ)ⲛ̄ⲧⲱⲛ-ⲩ 'whom we have likened (to him)' — i.e., 'those to whom we (might) compare him.' The sense is that Adam stands incomparable to anyone we could put alongside him in strength.

Tentatively parsed as Lyc. emphatic-reflexive ϩⲱⲟⲩ-ⲁⲛⲟⲩ 'they themselves' (cognate with Sah. ϩⲱⲟⲩ + intensive). Reading: Adam's contemporaries 'themselves were likewise in their years' — i.e., they too lived long lives, in contrast with today's diminished men.
